section_title: What is the warning in salt that no longer serves its purpose?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 34 Salt is good, but if the salt loses its savor, with what will it be seasoned? 35 It is fit neither for the soil nor for the manure pile, and it is thrown out. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

context_lines: Jesus closes the teaching about discipleship with the picture of salt. Salt is good, but salt that has lost its savor is no longer useful, even for the soil or the manure pile. It is thrown out.
The image follows the call to count the cost and give Him priority. It presses the question of what a follower’s life is actually doing, rather than whether someone merely travels with the crowd.
Jesus ends by calling those with ears to hear. The warning asks for attention and a response to the teaching that has just been given.
common_interpretation_lines: Christian readings commonly understand the salt as a picture of discipleship that must retain its purpose. The Catholic bishops’ notes connect it with the wholehearted commitment of the preceding sayings, while Wesley applies it to Christians and especially those who minister. ([USCCB note on Luke 14:34–35](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/luke/14); [Wesley on Luke 14:34](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-gospel-according-to-st-luke/))
god_plan_lines: Matthew records Jesus calling His disciples the salt of the earth and the light of the world, with good deeds that lead others to glorify the Father. That parallel gives the wider direction of a useful life: witness that makes God known. ([Matthew 5:13–16](https://biblehub.com/bsb/matthew/5.htm))

Colossians uses salt in another picture of that outward-facing life: wise conduct toward outsiders and gracious speech suited to each person. The images are related, without requiring that salt always carry one fixed meaning in every passage. ([Colossians 4:5–6](https://biblehub.com/bsb/colossians/4.htm))
